summary.text: Sunspots are temporary patches on the Sun's surface that look darker than their surroundings because they are cooler.
They form where concentrated magnetic fields block convection, and their number rises and falls with the roughly 11-year solar cycle.
They signal intense magnetic activity, and most solar flares and coronal mass ejections start in the active regions around them.

facts.label: Umbra temperature
facts.value: About 3000–4500 K, versus about 5780 K around it

facts.label: Lifetime
facts.value: A few days to a few months

facts.label: Earliest record
facts.value: China's I Ching, completed before 800 BC

items.prompt: Imagine lifting a single sunspot away from the Sun and viewing it alone against a black sky. How would it look?

options.label: Pitch black, giving off no light
Dimmer than the faintest star
A pale blue-white glow
Brighter than the full moon, crimson-orange

items.explain: A sunspot only looks dark beside the hotter surface; on its own it would shine brighter than the full moon with a crimson-orange color.

items.prompt: Why does a sunspot look dark against the rest of the Sun?

options.label: Magnetism blocks convection, so it is cooler
It is a hole showing a dark solar core
A cloud of dust drifts in front of it
A passing planet casts a shadow there

items.explain: A strong magnetic field inhibits convection, leaving the region cooler, and cooler gas there gives off far less light than the hotter surface.

items.prompt: William Herschel noticed that years with few sunspots matched years of high wheat prices in England. What has later analysis found?

options.label: Fewer sunspots reliably mean poorer harvests
More sunspots reliably mean poorer harvests
No statistically significant link exists
The link holds only for English wheat

items.explain: Carrington and Poynting failed to find a connection, and modern analysis finds no statistically significant correlation between wheat prices and sunspot numbers.

items.prompt: A sunspot has a very dark center surrounded by a lighter ring of streaky filaments. Where is its magnetic field strongest?

options.label: In the outer penumbra
In the central umbra
In the narrow light bridges
In the surface outside it

items.explain: The umbra is the darkest part, where the magnetic field is strongest and nearly vertical; the brighter penumbra has a more tilted field.

items.prompt: How could people in China record sunspots before 800 BC, long before telescopes existed?

options.label: They looked through polished crystal lenses
Larger spots can be seen with the naked eye
They only saw them during total eclipses
They inferred them from glowing aurorae

items.explain: Larger sunspots can be seen from Earth without a telescope, which is how the I Ching could record them before 800 BC.

items.prompt: Space-weather forecasters keep a close eye on large sunspot groups. Why?

options.label: Large groups shield Earth from solar wind
Large groups make the Sun's output drop sharply
Most flares and mass ejections start near them
Large groups mean the solar cycle is ending

items.explain: Most solar flares and coronal mass ejections come from the magnetically active regions around visible sunspot groups.

paragraphs.heading: Dark patches on the Sun
paragraphs.text: Sunspots are short-lived patches on the surface of the Sun that look darker than the area around them. They are cooler patches, where concentrated magnetic fields hold back convection. They usually appear in pairs with opposite magnetic polarity, and their number rises and falls over the solar cycle of about 11 years.

paragraphs.heading: Size and lifetime
paragraphs.text: A single sunspot or a group can last from a few days to a few months before it fades away. As they travel across the Sun, sunspots grow and shrink, ranging from 16 km to 160,000 km across. The biggest ones can be seen from Earth without a telescope. Most solar flares and coronal mass ejections start in the magnetically active regions around groups of sunspots.

paragraphs.heading: Umbra and penumbra
paragraphs.text: A sunspot has two main parts. The umbra is the darkest region, where the magnetic field is strongest and points almost straight out of the surface. Around it lies the penumbra, a brighter zone made of long filaments running outward, where the field is more tilted. The umbra is about 3000–4500 K, while the surface around it is about 5780 K, which is why the spot stands out as dark.

paragraphs.heading: Dark only by comparison
paragraphs.text: Set apart from the rest of the Sun, a single sunspot would actually shine brighter than the full moon, glowing crimson-orange. It looks dark only because the light given off by a hot surface like the Sun's changes greatly with temperature, so the cooler patch is much dimmer than its surroundings. Something called the Wilson effect also suggests that sunspots are hollows sitting lower than the surface around them.

paragraphs.heading: Watched for millennia
paragraphs.text: People have recorded sunspots for a very long time. The oldest record is in the Chinese I Ching, finished before 800 BC, and Chinese astronomers were noting sunspots regularly in imperial records by 28 BC. In the West, the Greek scholar Theophrastus mentioned one around 300 BC, and the monk John of Worcester drew the earliest known sketches in December 1128. The English astronomer Thomas Harriot first observed them through a telescope in December 1610, and Johannes and David Fabricius and Galileo followed soon after.

paragraphs.heading: Sunspots and wheat prices
paragraphs.text: Sunspots have also tempted people to look for links with life on Earth. In the early 19th century, William Herschel suspected sunspots were connected to Earth's temperatures. He noticed that a lack of sunspots from 1795 to 1800 matched high wheat prices in England. Later researchers, including Richard Carrington in 1865, failed to confirm the link, and modern analysis finds no statistically significant connection between wheat prices and sunspot numbers.
